findings.title: Duplicate definition of OptimizedImage.downsize silently overrides the width/height variant
findings.body: The file now defines `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and a second `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. In Ruby the later definition wins, so any existing caller that passes width and height separately (the signature kept at line 145 implies such callers exist, e.g. avatar/import paths) will actually hit the second method: `dimensions` receives the width and `opts` receives the height (an Integer). Inside `optimize`, `opts[:allow_animation]` is then called on an Integer, which raises `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer`, breaking every width/height-style downsize call at runtime. The first definition is dead code and the width/height calling convention is broken; either remove the old method and update all callers, or give the dimensions variant a different name.

findings.title: Hard-coded 10MB client limit ignores max_image_size_kb and max_attachment_size_kb site settings
findings.body: `validateUploadedFile` previously enforced `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, i.e. the admin-configured per-type limit (images vs attachments). It now always allows 10MB. For attachments there is no server-side downsizing, so on sites where `max_attachment_size_kb` is set below 10MB the client-side guard no longer rejects oversized files with the friendly size message; the upload is sent in full and then fails server-side with a generic error. It also ignores admins who raised limits above 10MB. Only image downsizing was added server-side; the attachment check should keep reading the site setting.

findings.title: Animated GIFs are flattened to a single frame when downsized because the extension check never matches tempfile paths
findings.body: `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) pipeline only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the paths passed from `create_upload` are Rack multipart tempfiles or `FileHelper.download` tempfiles, whose names have no `.gif` extension. Consequently any animated GIF larger than `max_image_size_kb` is processed by ImageMagick `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame: the user's animated upload is silently converted to a still image even when `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation-detection should be based on the original filename/content, not the tempfile path.

findings.title: 413 error message always claims the limit is 10 MB
findings.body: `displayErrorForUpload` reports a hard-coded "10 MB" maximum when the server returns 413, but the actual limit is `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb`, which the admin can set to anything. On sites with a different limit the message shown to users is factually wrong and confusing. The previous code read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` here.

findings.title: API URL download cap hard-coded to 10MB regresses sites with higher max_image_size_kb
findings.body: The remote-download size limit for API uploads was changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hard-coded `10.megabytes`. Sites that configured `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB can no longer pull images via URL larger than 10MB (they now silently fail with `rescue nil`, producing a confusing `tempfile`-nil path), while the client-facing intent of the PR is to allow large images that are then downsized. The cap should be derived from the setting (or at least max(setting, 10MB)).

findings.title: Downsizing loop runs up to 5 full ImageMagick + ImageOptim passes per upload and can still not converge
findings.body: Each iteration applies `-resize 80%`, which reduces area to ~64%, so five iterations shrink the image at most ~10x; an image far above the limit (e.g. 50MB against a 1MB setting) still exceeds it after the loop and then fails in `Upload.create_for` with a generic error. Additionally, when `downsize` returns false (convert failure), the return value is ignored, so the loop burns all 5 attempts doing nothing on the same file. Each pass also invokes ImageOptim, making this expensive CPU work on the request path for synchronous API uploads. The loop should stop early on failure and compute a resize percentage that reaches the target in one pass.
